bad.bus.default.message: The device transmits at 250 kbps; GLV CAN runs at 500 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 250 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

The device uses CAN 2.0B 29-bit identifiers; the bus is declared 11-bit. Mixed formats coexist electrically, but an extended frame costs 25 more bits than a standard one — 160 against 135 for eight data bytes — so the bus budget has to be recomputed with the right frame length, and every 29-bit frame loses arbitration to every 11-bit frame regardless of what the numbers mean.

bad.mount.cgf_only.0.001.message: Vehicle parameters are incomplete (mass_kg, wheelbase_m, mu_lat), so the yaw behaviour cannot be derived and generic FSAE numbers are used instead. Mass, wheelbase, CG position and measured lateral grip are four numbers the team already owns; supplying them replaces the only remaining guess in this calculation.

A 1153 mm offset from the CG produces up to 0.899 g of acceleration the car does not experience (+0.633 g longitudinal, -0.639 g lateral) in the slalom case (from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car) — rapid yaw reversal — the error peaks with steering input and therefore imitates real vehicle response. That is above the 0.00 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.882 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.172 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

That is above the 0.00 g you said you would accept. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.882 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. blocking.message: 20 Hz IMU against 15 Hz of chassis motion is below Nyquist. The aliased content is not noise — it is real motion folded to a frequency it never had, and nothing downstream can undo it.

The device transmits at 250 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 250 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.
The device needs 13-16 V and no declared rail sits in that window (5V 5V, 12V 12V). A 5 V sensor rail cannot power it; this needs the 12 V side or a dedicated regulator.

sensors.name: Chassis acceleration (IMU)
sensors.why: the measured side of every load case the suspension and aero models currently assert

sensors.name: Chassis angular rate (IMU)
sensors.why: yaw rate closes the loop on the handling model, and it is also what makes the lever-arm correction computable

sensors.name: GNSS position
sensors.why: lap segmentation and corner-by-corner comparison; without it every lap time is a single number with no structure

sensors.name: GNSS speed and heading
sensors.why: an absolute speed reference that does not depend on wheel speed, so it stays true under lock-up and wheelspin — which is exactly when wheel speed lies

Of that, 0.882 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.172 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

300 ms of velocity latency is 6.00 m of track at 20 m/s. Correct for it by time-shifting on a known event — a hard braking onset is visible in both the IMU and the GNSS velocity, and the offset between them is the number you need.
20 Hz IMU against 15 Hz of chassis motion is below Nyquist. The aliased content is not noise — it is real motion folded to a frequency it never had, and nothing downstream can undo it.

Position updates at 5 Hz and inertial data at 20 Hz — a 4:1 ratio. These must stay in separate CAN frames on separate identifiers. Sharing a frame forces the position data to the IMU rate, which does not make it fresher; it repeats stale values at 20 Hz, which looks like fast data and is not.

The device transmits at 250 kbps; GLV CAN runs at 500 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 250 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

The device uses CAN 2.0B 29-bit identifiers; the bus is declared 11-bit. Mixed formats coexist electrically, but an extended frame costs 25 more bits than a standard one — 160 against 135 for eight data bytes — so the bus budget has to be recomputed with the right frame length, and every 29-bit frame loses arbitration to every 11-bit frame regardless of what the numbers mean.
The device needs 13-16 V and no declared rail sits in that window (5V 5V, 12V 12V). A 5 V sensor rail cannot power it; this needs the 12 V side or a dedicated regulator.

open.message: 1 of 8 measurement questions are unanswered: Heading accuracy. These are the lines that decide what the data can be used for. Position accuracy decides whether a racing line is meaningful or whether consecutive laps just look different; heading resolution decides whether a slip-angle estimate is possible at all. Until they are filled in from the manual, this node is a purchase and not yet a channel.

Whether an external antenna is required is still an open question. It is not a small one: an external antenna adds a coaxial run, a ground-plane requirement and a mounting point that has to see the sky, which lands on chassis and on aero rather than on electrics.
No calibration procedure declared.

bare.mount.cgf_only.0.001.message: Vehicle parameters are incomplete (mass_kg, wheelbase_m, mu_lat), so the yaw behaviour cannot be derived and generic FSAE numbers are used instead. Mass, wheelbase, CG position and measured lateral grip are four numbers the team already owns; supplying them replaces the only remaining guess in this calculation.

The mounting offset from the centre of gravity has not been measured. 'As close to the CG as possible' is a preference, not a specification, and without the actual vector the rotational terms cannot be subtracted in post — which means whatever offset exists stays in the data permanently. Measuring it is a tape measure and five minutes; recovering from not having measured it is not possible after the session.

findings.message: Measurement questions answered: Tight node 100%, Bare 0%. Both start low, and that is the honest state — but the bought unit's answers exist in a manual and can be transcribed this afternoon, whereas the DIY figures do not exist anywhere until the board is built and bench tested. Those two kinds of blank are not the same size.

The trade is calibration effort against integration effort. The COTS unit arrives with a fixed bitrate and a fixed frame layout you must accommodate, and it is the reason the bitrate conflict above exists at all. The DIY node lets you choose the bitrate, the identifiers and the update rates to fit the bus you already have, and in exchange you own the GNSS driver, the IMU fusion, the enclosure, the connector termination and every accuracy figure — none of which are hard individually, all of which are a term's work together. If the team already runs Teensy 4.1 with FlexCAN_T4 elsewhere, the firmware side is genuinely cheaper than it looks; the sensor characterisation is not.
Tight node is $300 before the antenna and the mating connector (DT06-4S). Deutsch DT terminations also need the right crimp tool, which is a real line item the first time.

cots.bus.default.message: The device transmits at 1000 kbps; GLV CAN runs at 500 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 1000 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

The device uses CAN 2.0B 29-bit identifiers; the bus is declared 11-bit. Mixed formats coexist electrically, but an extended frame costs 25 more bits than a standard one — 160 against 135 for eight data bytes — so the bus budget has to be recomputed with the right frame length, and every 29-bit frame loses arbitration to every 11-bit frame regardless of what the numbers mean.

cots.bus.fast_ext.message: Device and DAQ CAN both at 1000 kbps.

A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 1000 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

The device uses CAN 2.0B 29-bit identifiers; the bus is declared 11-bit. Mixed formats coexist electrically, but an extended frame costs 25 more bits than a standard one — 160 against 135 for eight data bytes — so the bus budget has to be recomputed with the right frame length, and every 29-bit frame loses arbitration to every 11-bit frame regardless of what the numbers mean.

These are the lines that decide what the data can be used for. Position accuracy decides whether a racing line is meaningful or whether consecutive laps just look different; heading resolution decides whether a slip-angle estimate is possible at all. Whether an external antenna is required is still an open question. It is not a small one: an external antenna adds a coaxial run, a ground-plane requirement and a mounting point that has to see the sky, which lands on chassis and on aero rather than on electrics.

Measuring it is a tape measure and five minutes; recovering from not having measured it is not possible after the session.

Velocity latency is not declared. GNSS velocity is a filtered quantity and lags reality by substantially more than the IMU does, so fusing the two without knowing the offset time-shifts one against the other. At competition speeds a tenth of a second is metres of track, and a lap-position trace built from a lagged velocity puts every event in the wrong corner.
Supply current not declared — the rail budget cannot include it.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 1000 kbps; GLV CAN runs at 500 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 1000 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

open.message: 8 of 8 measurement questions are unanswered: Velocity accuracy, Velocity maximum, Velocity resolution, Velocity latency, Position accuracy, Height accuracy, Heading accuracy, Heading resolution. Whether an external antenna is required is still an open question. It is not a small one: an external antenna adds a coaxial run, a ground-plane requirement and a mounting point that has to see the sky, which lands on chassis and on aero rather than on electrics.

The mounting offset from the centre of gravity has not been measured. 'As close to the CG as possible' is a preference, not a specification, and without the actual vector the rotational terms cannot be subtracted in post — which means whatever offset exists stays in the data permanently. At competition speeds a tenth of a second is metres of track, and a lap-position trace built from a lagged velocity puts every event in the wrong corner.
Supply current not declared — the rail budget cannot include it.

edges.mount.cgf_only.0.001.message: Vehicle parameters are incomplete (mass_kg, wheelbase_m, mu_lat), so the yaw behaviour cannot be derived and generic FSAE numbers are used instead. Mass, wheelbase, CG position and measured lateral grip are four numbers the team already owns; supplying them replaces the only remaining guess in this calculation.

A 374 mm offset from the CG produces up to 0.263 g of acceleration the car does not experience (-0.129 g longitudinal, +0.229 g lateral) in the slalom case (from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car) — rapid yaw reversal — the error peaks with steering input and therefore imitates real vehicle response. That is above the 0.00 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.258 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.050 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

open.message: 8 of 8 measurement questions are unanswered: Velocity accuracy, Velocity maximum, Velocity resolution, Velocity latency, Position accuracy, Height accuracy, Heading accuracy, Heading resolution. These are the lines that decide what the data can be used for. Position accuracy decides whether a racing line is meaningful or whether consecutive laps just look different; heading resolution decides whether a slip-angle estimate is possible at all. Until they are filled in from the manual, this node is a purchase and not yet a channel.

Whether an external antenna is required is still an open question. It is not a small one: an external antenna adds a coaxial run, a ground-plane requirement and a mounting point that has to see the sky, which lands on chassis and on aero rather than on electrics.
No calibration procedure declared.

The mounting offset from the centre of gravity has not been measured. 'As close to the CG as possible' is a preference, not a specification, and without the actual vector the rotational terms cannot be subtracted in post — which means whatever offset exists stays in the data permanently. Measuring it is a tape measure and five minutes; recovering from not having measured it is not possible after the session.

Velocity latency is not declared. GNSS velocity is a filtered quantity and lags reality by substantially more than the IMU does, so fusing the two without knowing the offset time-shifts one against the other. At competition speeds a tenth of a second is metres of track, and a lap-position trace built from a lagged velocity puts every event in the wrong corner.

100 Hz IMU is 6.7x the 15 Hz chassis bandwidth.

sensors.name: Chassis acceleration (IMU)
sensors.why: the measured side of every load case the suspension and aero models currently assert

sensors.name: Chassis angular rate (IMU)
sensors.why: yaw rate closes the loop on the handling model, and it is also what makes the lever-arm correction computable

sensors.name: GNSS position
sensors.why: lap segmentation and corner-by-corner comparison; without it every lap time is a single number with no structure

sensors.name: GNSS speed and heading
sensors.why: an absolute speed reference that does not depend on wheel speed, so it stays true under lock-up and wheelspin — which is exactly when wheel speed lies

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; slow runs at 125 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

hog12.mount.cgf_only.0.001.message: Vehicle parameters are incomplete (mass_kg, wheelbase_m, mu_lat), so the yaw behaviour cannot be derived and generic FSAE numbers are used instead. Mass, wheelbase, CG position and measured lateral grip are four numbers the team already owns; supplying them replaces the only remaining guess in this calculation.

A 374 mm offset from the CG produces up to 0.263 g of acceleration the car does not experience (-0.129 g longitudinal, +0.229 g lateral) in the slalom case (from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car) — rapid yaw reversal — the error peaks with steering input and therefore imitates real vehicle response. That is above the 0.00 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.258 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.050 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

A 374 mm offset from the CG produces up to 0.263 g of acceleration the car does not experience (-0.129 g longitudinal, +0.229 g lateral) in the slalom case (from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car) — rapid yaw reversal — the error peaks with steering input and therefore imitates real vehicle response. That is above the 0.05 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.258 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.050 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

That is above the 0.05 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.258 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.050 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

derived_from_declared_vehicle: yaw rate from the grip limit, omega = v / R with R = v^2 / (mu g)
peak yaw acceleration from one axle saturated laterally, M_z = mu m g (b/L) a, divided by yaw inertia — which reduces to alpha_max = mu g / L under the dynamic-index-one inertia estimate
VehicleSpec.manoeuvres() replaces the generic MANOEUVRES entirely once mass, wheelbase, CG position and measured grip are declared, and every finding states which basis it used
estimate_flagged: yaw inertia defaults to the dynamic-index-one approximation I_zz ~= m a b; a bifilar swing test replaces it and the finding says so explicitly whenever the estimate was used

MANOEUVRES is a FALLBACK only, used when no VehicleSpec is supplied. Findings computed from it are labelled 'from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car' in their own message text, so the label travels with the number into any document it is pasted into
default tolerance_g = 0.05 is a judgement about what is worth correcting, not a physical threshold
vehicle_bandwidth_hz = 15 Hz is a generic chassis figure
from_documentation: position 25 Hz, IMU 100 Hz, CAN 1 Mbps, CAN 2.0B
Deutsch DT06-4S / DT15-4P, mating part F02U.B00.656-01
calibration by USB, zeroed stationary on a flat surface
mounting requirement: as close to the centre of gravity as possible
provenance.hard_rule: Every measurement question stays Optional and every blank is reported individually. A spec sheet that lists 'velocity accuracy' as a heading has not stated a velocity accuracy, and the difference between those two is the difference between a channel and a purchase.
physics_grounded: lever-arm error from planar rigid-body kinematics, a_meas = a_cg + alpha x r + omega x (omega x r), yaw axis only
latency expressed as distance travelled, v * t
Nyquist applied to the IMU rate against declared chassis bandwidth
CAN frame length via daq_plan.can_frame_bits (ISO 11898-1 layout), so the 29-bit identifier cost is computed rather than asserted

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. tight.mount.full.0.001.message: Peak yaw acceleration derived from the declared car: 10.1 rad/s^2, from one axle saturated at mu = 1.6 over a 1.55 m wheelbase, with yaw inertia estimated as m*a*b = 168 kg m^2 (dynamic index 1). A bifilar swing test replaces that estimate.

A 22 mm offset from the CG produces up to 0.021 g of acceleration the car does not experience (-0.005 g longitudinal, +0.021 g lateral) in the transient 10 m/s case (derived from the declared vehicle) — yaw reversal at the tyre limit — the error peaks with steering input and therefore imitates real vehicle response. That is above the 0.00 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

Of that, 0.021 g comes from yaw acceleration rather than steady cornering. This part is phase-locked to steering input, so on a plot it is indistinguishable from genuine vehicle response and will not be spotted by inspection. The steady centripetal part (0.005 g) is the easy one — it looks like a zero offset and someone will eventually 'fix' it by re-zeroing, which removes the evidence without removing the error.

blocking.message: The device transmits at 500 kbps; DAQ CAN runs at 1000 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.

sensors.name: Chassis acceleration (IMU)
sensors.why: the measured side of every load case the suspension and aero models currently assert

sensors.name: Chassis angular rate (IMU)
sensors.why: yaw rate closes the loop on the handling model, and it is also what makes the lever-arm correction computable

sensors.name: GNSS position
sensors.why: lap segmentation and corner-by-corner comparison; without it every lap time is a single number with no structure

sensors.name: GNSS speed and heading
sensors.why: an absolute speed reference that does not depend on wheel speed, so it stays true under lock-up and wheelspin — which is exactly when wheel speed lies

That is above the 0.01 g you said you would accept. Two ways out, and the second is usually the real one: move the unit closer to the CG, or record the offset vector and subtract alpha x r + omega x (omega x r) in post using the yaw rate this same device already reports. The correction is arithmetic; what makes it fail is not knowing the offset.

5 ms of velocity latency is 0.15 m of track at 30 m/s. Correct for it by time-shifting on a known event — a hard braking onset is visible in both the IMU and the GNSS velocity, and the offset between them is the number you need.
500 Hz IMU is 12.5x the 40 Hz chassis bandwidth.

Position updates at 50 Hz and inertial data at 500 Hz — a 10:1 ratio. These must stay in separate CAN frames on separate identifiers. Sharing a frame forces the position data to the IMU rate, which does not make it fresher; it repeats stale values at 500 Hz, which looks like fast data and is not.

The device transmits at 500 kbps; slow runs at 125 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.
4.5-30 V window is met by 5V, 12V. The wide window means unregulated GLV is acceptable, so this does not need its own regulator and does not brown out on a crank.

findings.message: 0 mm from the CG — worst-case spurious acceleration 0.000 g (from GENERIC FSAE manoeuvre numbers, not this car), inside the 0.01 g tolerance.

0 ms of velocity latency is 0.00 m of track at 30 m/s. Correct for it by time-shifting on a known event — a hard braking onset is visible in both the IMU and the GNSS velocity, and the offset between them is the number you need.
200 Hz IMU is 5.0x the 40 Hz chassis bandwidth.

Position updates at 20 Hz and inertial data at 200 Hz — a 10:1 ratio. These must stay in separate CAN frames on separate identifiers. Sharing a frame forces the position data to the IMU rate, which does not make it fresher; it repeats stale values at 200 Hz, which looks like fast data and is not.

The device transmits at 500 kbps; slow runs at 125 kbps. These do not partially work. A node at the wrong bitrate cannot win arbitration or acknowledge a frame, so it error-frames continuously and degrades the bus for every other node — the symptom is the rest of the car misbehaving, which sends people looking anywhere but here. Three ways out: reconfigure the device if it supports it, run the vehicle bus at 500 kbps, or give it its own bus and gateway the frames across on the logger.
7-18 V window is met by 12V. The wide window means unregulated GLV is acceptable, so this does not need its own regulator and does not brown out on a crank.

rate.message: 200 Hz IMU is 13.3x the 15 Hz chassis bandwidth.

Position updates at 20 Hz and inertial data at 200 Hz — a 10:1 ratio. These must stay in separate CAN frames on separate identifiers. Sharing a frame forces the position data to the IMU rate, which does not make it fresher; it repeats stale values at 200 Hz, which looks like fast data and is not.

rate60.message: 200 Hz IMU is only 3.3x the 60 Hz of interest. Above Nyquist but below the ~5x where peaks stop being clipped by sampling phase.
